ruling.recommended_action: Uphold the $6.61 cancellation fee (no refund); no account action against either party.
ruling.reasoning:
The dispute enters the NS group through NS-0: the cancellation is driver-side on a no-show claim, so it is NS-1/NS-2 that govern, not NS-3/NS-4 [F4][NS-0]. The execution trace settles all three NS-1 elements: the driver tapped "I'm Here" at 14:06:15, which is (i) [F6][F4][NS-1]; at that moment he was 178 m from the pickup, inside the 200 m arrival radius, which is (ii) [F6][F1][NS-1]; and he then stayed continuously inside that radius for 220 s (3 min 40 s) until he cancelled at 14:09:55, which exceeds the 180 s threshold of (iii) [F6][F2][F4][NS-1]. Nothing in the record defeats any of the three: the GPS trace runs from the arrival confirmation to the cancellation with no hole, so there is no G12 gap to send to a person [F2][F6][NS-1].

The rider's case is that the fee should not stand because the driver stopped 179 m short at a side road rather than at the named entrance [F1][F3][F10]. That is a real factual reading of the record — his closest approach was 40 m at 14:03:50 and he was then stationary 14:05:55–14:09:55 at 179 m, and his own message places him "at the side road" [F1][F3][F9]. But NS-1 does not make touching the pin an element; its arrival test is the driver being at the pick-up location according to GPS, operationalised as being within the pickup radius at the moment of the arrival confirmation, which is exactly what the trace marks ✓ [F6][F1][NS-1]. The rider's advocate herself conceded on rebuttal that the mechanical test was satisfied, and withdrew the timeline-based claim [F6][F3][NS-2]. The driver's post-trip statement that he was "parked at the pickup" [F13] is contradicted by GPS [F3] and is given no weight, but the driver's case does not depend on it: the fee stands on the system record alone, and system records prevail over statements [F6][F3][F13][NS-1].

Because (i), (ii) and (iii) are all satisfied, the $6.61 charge is the rider's liability under NS-1 and NS-2 is not triggered — NS-2 applies only where one of the NS-1 elements fails [F4][F7][F6][NS-1][NS-2]. The amount is a published fee with no surge multiplier, so FARE-1 requires no reduction of any other item either [F7][F8][FARE-1]. The correct outcome is therefore no_action, and no amount is refunded [F4][F7][NS-1]. The driver's 90-day record (1 dispute, 1 upheld on no-show) is a profile fact and cannot decide the case, and because the case is not established against the driver (no refund and no RD-1 breach), RD-6 does not attach an account flag; the rider's own profile shows 0 upheld disputes [F18][F17][RD-6][NS-1].

Safety screen: I read the complaint, all three chat messages and the driver's statement [F9][F10][F11][F12][F13]. Chat #1 is a pickup-location notice, #2 reports the rider's position, #3 announces the cancellation after a wait; the statement is a factual account of parking and waiting. No threat, intimidation, harassment, sexual remark or dangerous-driving allegation appears, so safety_concern is "none" [F9][F10][F11][F13][SAFE-1]. The evidence is sufficient: every element of the ruling rests on a system record the trace marks settled (GPS, timeline, fare) with no missing or untimed message [F2][F3][F4][F6][F7][F12]. The case type is no-show, not route deviation, so segment_findings is empty [F4][NS-0].

rejected_claims.reason: Accepted as a correct statement of the record — the tap at 14:06:15 was 178 m from the pickup, inside the 200 m radius [F6] — and it therefore supports NS-1(ii), not the rider's refund: NS-1 fixes that radius as the arrival test [NS-1].

The distance facts are accurate — closest approach 40 m at 14:03:50, then stationary 179 m away [F1][F3] — but distance from the pin is not an NS-1 element; the arrival test is being within the pickup radius at the moment of confirmation, which is met [F6][NS-1].

It is true the driver stayed on the side road and the rider waited at the entrance [F9][F10][F3], but NS-1(iii) requires the driver to wait at the pickup location for over 3 minutes, which the record shows (220 s inside the radius after the tap) [F6][NS-1]; the rider's message does not defeat the recorded wait.

Accepted and applied: the driver's statement of being 'at the pickup' [F13] is outweighed by the GPS position 179 m out [F3], per the rule that system records prevail over statements; but the fee stands on the GPS/timeline record without the statement [F6][F3][NS-1].

Correct that fair weather and no incidents [F15][F16] remove any reroute justification, but RD-4 justification is irrelevant to an NS no-show assessment; none of the driver's NS-1 elements depends on a reasonable-cause excuse [NS-1].
Rejected: NS-1 makes the $6.61 the rider's liability precisely because (i)–(iii) are satisfied [F6][F4][NS-1]; NS-2 applies only where an NS-1 element fails, and none does [NS-1][NS-2].

Rejected: RD-6 attaches a flag only where the case is established against the driver (refund > 0 or an RD-1 breach); here no fee is refunded and no RD-1 breach is recorded, so the driver's one prior upheld no-show dispute [F18] cannot ground an account referral [F18][RD-6].

Accepted: $6.61 with no surge [F7][F8] is the published figure and FARE-1 adds nothing to refund; but the rider's dispute is entitlement under NS-1/NS-2, not quantum, and NS-1 makes the fee valid [FARE-1][NS-1].
Accepted as an accurate reading of the chats [F9][F10][F11]; the notice and cancellation are consistent with a completed NS-1 wait [F6][NS-1].

Accepted that the chat record is complete — 3 timestamped messages [F12] — so no G12 gap arises; the driver's statement is not relied on but the system record independently satisfies NS-1 [F6][F3][NS-1].
